nameStory: This little sea star gets its name from its slender, narrow arms that are much thinner than most other sea stars you'll encounter. The 'green' part comes from its typical olive-green to brownish-green coloration, though it can sometimes appear more grayish. It's like nature designed a more delicate, streamlined version of the classic chunky sea stars we usually picture.
description: The Green Slender Sea Star is a small, delicate sea star with five notably thin arms radiating from a small central disc. It typically grows to about 2-3 inches across, making it one of the smaller sea stars in New England waters. Its body has a smooth, somewhat leathery texture and ranges from olive-green to brownish-green in color. Unlike the plump, cushiony arms of larger sea stars, this species looks almost spindly by comparison.

idTips.label: Slender Arms
idTips.description: The arms are noticeably thin and narrow compared to other sea stars - about 3-4 times longer than they are wide, giving it an almost spidery appearance

idTips.label: Small Size
idTips.description: Usually measures 2-3 inches across when fully extended, fitting easily in the palm of your hand

idTips.label: Green Coloration
idTips.description: Typically olive-green to brownish-green on top, sometimes with a grayish tint, and paler underneath

idTips.label: Smooth Texture
idTips.description: Feels smooth and leathery to the touch, lacking the bumpy or spiny texture of many other sea stars

idTips.label: Small Central Disc
idTips.description: The body center is quite small relative to the arm length, making the arms appear to emerge from a tiny hub

habitat: Look for Green Slender Sea Stars in rocky intertidal zones and shallow subtidal areas along New England's coast, typically under rocks, in crevices, or among seaweed. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are often found in tide pools or just below the low tide mark. They're more common in the cooler waters of northern New England.

seasonality.spring: Active in tide pools as water temperatures begin to warm. This is a good time to spot them moving around during low tide exploration.
seasonality.summer: Most active and easiest to find during summer low tides. They may be found feeding on small mollusks and other prey in shallow waters.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may begin moving to slightly deeper water. Continue checking under rocks in protected tide pools.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and harder to find as they retreat to deeper, more protected waters to avoid harsh winter conditions.

funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, Green Slender Sea Stars can completely regenerate a lost arm - and amazingly, if the arm breaks off with enough of the central disc attached, the severed arm can actually grow an entirely new sea star body, essentially creating a clone of itself!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with juvenile common sea stars, but remember the key difference: even baby common sea stars have proportionally thicker, more robust arms. Think 'skinny adult' versus 'chunky baby' - the Green Slender Sea Star stays skinny even when fully grown.
contextualKnowledge: This species is quite rare in New England waters, representing the southern edge of its range - it's much more common in the colder waters of Atlantic Canada and the Arctic, so finding one here is actually quite special.
compareHints: **Note: Limited observation data (only 2 recorded) suggests this identification should be verified by experts.** Compared to the much more common Common Sea Star (Asterias species), the Green Slender Sea Star is significantly smaller and has much thinner arms relative to its body size. While Common Sea Stars have thick, fleshy arms and can grow quite large, this species maintains its delicate, spindly appearance throughout its life.
